chapters.title: 5.1 Network Interception & Mocking
chapters.overviewText: cy.intercept() patches window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest before app JS runs, which is why the intercept must be registered before the action that triggers the request. One API covers three jobs: spy (observe, real response through), stub (replace the response), and modify in-flight. Omit the method and you match every HTTP verb on that URL — a silent alias bug. Most-recently-registered intercept wins; GraphQL matches on req.body.operationName, not the URL.
chapters.why: Intercept-after-visit is the single most common cy.intercept() mistake. Interviewers also expect you to distinguish spy vs stub vs modify, explain method-required matching, and know that Cypress matches the newest intercept first — the reverse of 'first match wins' intuition.
chapters.when: Before stubbing leave-list, employee, or GraphQL endpoints. Revisit when a loading spinner is too fast to assert, when two intercepts fight, or when POST /graphql needs per-operation aliases.

practical.scenario: Leave list must show loading, empty, 500, and retry states; GraphQL traffic all hits POST /graphql.
practical.pass: You register intercepts before cy.visit, specify GET vs POST, stub with { fixture }, delay a real response to catch the skeleton, re-register on retry, and alias GraphQL by operationName.
practical.fail: You intercept after visit, omit the method so a POST steals the GET alias, or match GraphQL only on the URL.

chapters.customSummary:
- Works by patching window.fetch/XMLHttpRequest in-page before app JS runs (Part 0.5) — which is exactly why intercepts must always be registered before the triggering action; registering after means Cypress never sees the call. The single most common mistake with this command
- Three distinct purposes under one API: spying (observe, let the real response through), stubbing (replace the response entirely), and modifying in-flight (req.continue()/req.reply() on a real request/response)
- Route matching: method + exact path, */** wildcards, regex, or a full matcher object ({ method, url, query, headers })
- Omitting the method matches ALL HTTP methods on that URL — a frequent silent bug (a GET-intended alias also catches the POST). Always specify the method explicitly
- Stubbing: static object/array, shorthand body-only (assumes 200), explicit statusCode/headers/body, { forceNetworkError: true } for connectivity failures, and { fixture: '...' } as the standard pairing with Part 5.2
- Dynamic responses via a handler function — inspect req.url/req.body, then req.reply(...)
- req.continue((res) => {...}) modifies a REAL response (inject data, force res.setDelay(ms)) — the deliberate-delay technique is the reliable way to make fast-resolving loading states observable on demand, rather than racing a sub-50ms real response
- Route precedence: most-recently-registered intercept wins, falling back to earlier/more-general ones — register broad stubs first, specific overrides second (the reverse of naive "first match" intuition)
- Selective pass-through: branch inside a handler (req.continue() for some cases, req.reply() for others) based on request content
- cy.wait('@alias') return value: .request.{method,url,headers,body}, .response.{statusCode,body,headers} — full inspection surface
- Call-count assertions: cy.get('@alias.all').should('have.length', n) without waiting again; asserting zero calls is a genuine, useful negative check (e.g., confirming Cancel doesn't fire a request)
- cy.wait(['@a','@b','@c']) — wait for several parallel on-load requests instead of guessing a delay
- Bundle related intercepts into a reusable custom command (cy.interceptLeaveApi()) — a recurring real-project pattern
- GraphQL: match on req.body.operationName inside a single POST /graphql handler, not on the URL; set req.alias dynamically
- vs Playwright: genuinely comparable, not a clear win either way — page.route()/fulfill()/continue() map almost 1:1 onto stub/continue. Cypress's named cy.wait('@alias') is terser; Playwright's predicate-based waitForResponse() is more flexible for complex matching. vs Selenium: no native interception at all — requires an external MITM proxy (BrowserMob, mitmproxy) bolted onto the WebDriver session; a concrete, practical reason teams move off Selenium for network-dependent UI work

chapters.title: 5.2 Fixtures
chapters.overviewText: cy.fixture() is a parent command that loads static files from cypress/fixtures — JSON by default, plus binary with { encoding: null }. Fixtures play three roles: mock intercept bodies (the dominant use), form input data, and expected-value assertions. Cypress.env() is configuration and secrets; fixtures are committed test/mock data. Never put credentials in a fixture or mock API bodies in cypress.env.json.
chapters.why: A flat fixtures/ folder of 40 files collapses. Mixing env secrets with mock payloads is a recurring beginner mistake, and generating random fixtures inside setupNodeEvents makes runs non-deterministic.
chapters.when: When pairing intercepts with mock bodies, driving onboarding forms from files, or deciding whether a value belongs in env or fixtures.

practical.scenario: You need pending/empty/error leave payloads, a unique email per create, and admin credentials for login.
practical.pass: You organize fixtures/leave-requests/{pending,empty,error-response}.json, mutate a canonical fixture for uniqueness, and keep passwords in Cypress.env().
practical.fail: You dump everything into one employees.json, commit real passwords into fixtures, or regenerate faker data on every run via setupNodeEvents.

chapters.customSummary:
- cy.fixture(name) — a parent command, .json assumed, subfolders supported, binary via { encoding: null } (Part 3.7 covers uploads)
- Three roles: (1) mock response bodies for cy.intercept() — the dominant real-world use; (2) input data to drive a test's form-filling; (3) expected-value data kept out of the spec file for assertions
- Organize by feature/endpoint in subfolders (employees/list.json, leave-requests/pending.json, .../empty.json, .../error-response.json) rather than one flat directory — scales far better past a handful of files
- Mutate loaded fixture data before use to cover variations from one canonical file (map over it, inject Date.now()-based uniqueness) rather than hand-maintaining near-duplicate files
- Combine multiple fixtures via nested .then() or — better, past two levels — via aliasing each and merging in one flattened .then(function(){ this.x }) (Part 2.5's pyramid-flattening pattern)
- Cypress.env() (config/secrets) vs fixtures (test/mock data) is a real, frequently-confused distinction — credentials belong in env, API response bodies belong in fixtures; never commit real credentials into a fixture, never put mock API bodies into cypress.env.json
- Generate large/repetitive fixture data with an external one-time script (e.g. @faker-js/faker), output committed as a static file — do NOT generate random fixture content inside setupNodeEvents on every run, which breaks determinism. Genuinely-fresh-per-run data is a cy.task() job, not a fixture
- Environment-aware fixture paths (fixtures/leave-requests/${env}/pending.json) are available but add indirection — use only when staging/local data genuinely must differ
- TypeScript: cy.fixture<Employee[]>(...) pays off directly for typed assertions and payloads
- vs Playwright: no dedicated fixture-loading command needed — test code already runs in Node, so a plain import or fs.readFileSync suffices; simpler, but no single verb signals "this is test data" the way cy.fixture() does. Naming collision to flag: Playwright separately uses "fixture" for its DI test-setup mechanism — an unrelated concept. vs Selenium: no fixture concept at all — whatever your language/framework's data-loading facilities provide (again a different "fixture" in pytest/TestNG)

chapters.title: 5.3 Aliases for Elements, Requests, and Data
chapters.overviewText: Aliases are the connective tissue between fixtures, intercepts, and the DOM. cy.get('@name') looks identical for all three kinds — Cypress tracks which kind was aliased. cy.wait() only works on network aliases. Naming a fixture @getLeave and then cy.wait('@getLeave') errors. Prefix data aliases (@leaveFixture vs @getLeave) so the name signals the category.
chapters.why: Once intercepts and fixtures mix, alias naming collisions become a real bug class. The alias system is also the ergonomic win that keeps a fixture+intercept+DOM triad readable instead of a nested .then() pyramid.
chapters.when: When a beforeEach loads a fixture, stubs an intercept from that data, and aliases rendered rows — and whenever cy.wait() unexpectedly fails on what you thought was a network alias.

practical.scenario: Manager approvals: fixture of pending requests, stub GET from that data, alias rows, approve, then re-check status.
practical.pass: You use @pendingRequests (data), @getLeave/@approveLeave (network), @leaveRows (element), wait only on network aliases, and rely on element-alias re-query after approval.
practical.fail: You name the fixture @getLeave and cy.wait('@getLeave'), or treat @leaveRows as a frozen snapshot from beforeEach.

chapters.customSummary:
- Consolidates Part 2.5's three alias kinds specifically in the networking context — the alias namespace for intercepts is separate from element/data aliases, even though cy.get('@name') syntax is identical for all three; Cypress tracks which kind was originally aliased
- cy.wait('@x') (waits) vs cy.get('@x') (retrieves without waiting) vs cy.get('@x.all')/cy.get('@x.1') (all calls / a specific call by index)
- Aliases compose across categories: cy.wait('@getLeave').its('response.body').as('leaveData') takes a network alias, extracts data from it, and creates a brand-new data alias — from that point cy.get('@leaveData') yields the plain value, not interception metadata
- The realistic combined pattern: fixture → data alias; data alias piped into cy.intercept() → network alias; rendered rows → element alias — all three set up in one beforeEach, keeping the test body itself clean
- Element aliases re-query on use (Part 2.5), which is what makes "wait for the network call, then re-check the SAME element alias" correctly reflect post-update DOM rather than a stale beforeEach snapshot
- Dynamically-generated alias names (@employee${id}) are legitimate for data-driven scenarios (Part 9.14) but trade away some readability — use only when the dynamism earns its keep
- The specific new gotcha here: naming a fixture (data) alias the same way as a network alias (e.g., both called @getLeave) invites a real bug — cy.wait() only works on network aliases and errors on a data alias. Convention fix: distinguish names by suffix (@leaveFixture vs @getLeave) so the alias name itself signals its category
- The payoff, restated: the alias system is what keeps a fixture+intercept+DOM triad readable as one flow instead of a deeply nested .then() pyramid — a distinctly Cypress ergonomic advantage once a test coordinates all three data sources simultaneously
